4: Purpose: find out whether you can handle Three Kings Day before it arrives, and how much money each campaign ties up.
6: 1. "Settings" sheet: first, the capacity of your production kitchen in pieces per hour. That number comes from the "Bottleneck" sheet of kitchen-capacity-and-site.xlsx in this same pack: open it, see which machine limits you and copy its pieces per hour here. It comes with a default value so the workbook works from the first minute, but it's an ASSUMPTION, not your production kitchen.
7: 2. "6-Peak Calendar" sheet: six campaigns with their star product, their days, their price and the units you expect to sell per day inside and outside the campaign. It's the only sheet where you type sales expectations.
8: 3. "Share of the Year" sheet: spread your annual sales across the twelve months and you'll see what percentage of the year is at stake in each campaign. It's the number that decides whether a campaign is worth setting up.
9: 4. "Peak Capacity vs Demand" sheet: this is the question of the workbook. Peak demand is your normal-day pieces times the campaign factor; capacity is the hours you can keep the production kitchen running. If there's a shortfall, you have three levers, in this order: more machine hours, production made ahead and frozen, and extra staff.
10: 5. "Extra Staff and Cash" sheet: what the extra staff costs at the real employer cost (base pay plus payroll taxes, workers' comp and benefits) and, above all, how much money the campaign's ingredient purchase ties up and for how many days. That money leaves your account weeks before the first dollar of the campaign comes in.
11: 6. Repeat the cycle every January with the real figures from the campaign you just closed: the workbook is only worth what you put into it, which is what really happened, not what you expected to happen.

13: What to know before you start
14: WHAT THIS WORKBOOK DOES AND WHAT YOUR TASK CALENDAR DOES. Your annual task calendar sets the DATES and what to do in each campaign, and your daily task checklists carry the detail of each event. This workbook doesn't repeat that calendar: it puts DOLLARS on it and answers "can I handle it?". They're two different pieces of the same problem, and you use them together.
15: There isn't a single formula here that points to another file. When a figure lives in another workbook of the pack (the production kitchen's capacity, for example), it's COPIED by hand and the note says so. A link between files breaks as soon as someone moves a folder, and then the workbook lies without telling you.
16: The campaign factor multiplies the pieces of the WHOLE PRODUCTION KITCHEN, not those of the star product. In a measured kitchen, individual pastries went from 50-60 pieces a day to 500-600 in the campaign with the same equipment. The 6.0 for Three Kings Day in the example is the only one that reaches that range; the rest stay between 1.6 and 2.6 because they're two-, three- or four-day campaigns.
17: A cream-filled rosca carries the 41 °F cold-holding limit (Food Code 3-501.16) and date marking (3-501.17) right on the biggest production day. That limits the campaign as much as the oven does: what you can't make ahead and freeze, you have to make the same day. The "Egg & TCS Decision" sheet of opening-menu-and-recipe-costing.xlsx tells you which item falls in that bag and which doesn't.
18: Made-ahead production has a physical ceiling that isn't on this sheet: the cubic feet of your freezer and the capacity of your blast chiller. Before you accept a made-ahead piece count, check that it fits. A chest freezer preserves but does NOT chill fast enough: it doesn't replace the blast chiller (Food Code cooling rule, 3-501.14).
19: Campaign cash is the number that surprises people most. You order raw materials weeks ahead, pay cash or at 30 days, and get paid when you sell. In between there's idle money that isn't in any income statement but is in your bank account.
20: How often to use this workbook: the "Settings" and the "6-Peak Calendar," ONCE A YEAR, in January, when you close the Three Kings Day campaign and have the data fresh. "Peak Capacity vs Demand" and "Extra Staff and Cash," ONCE PER CAMPAIGN, with the purchase lead time the sheet itself gives: for Three Kings Day, six weeks ahead, that is, late November.
21: To edit the structure or a cell that isn't green, unprotect the sheet: Review > Unprotect Sheet. The protection has NO password; it only stops you from overwriting a formula by accident.
